$comment: THE FORMULA EVAL CORPUS — the hand-written half.
Each task states a request a person would make, a fixture as typed cell
text, the formula that answers it, and the answer Calcula's own engine
produces. A `distractor` names the plausible wrong formula a model
reaches for and MUST NOT satisfy the expectation; a task whose
distractor also passes measures nothing and is a defect.
Every reference and every distractor in this file has been run through
Formulas are INVARIANT: comma separators, dot decimals.

tasks.intent: In the sales table in A1:C10, add up the Amount for every row where the Region is North AND the Rep is Alice. Rows that match only one of the two conditions must be excluded. Put the total in E2.

distractor.why: The single-condition SUMIF applies only the Region test and ignores the Rep entirely, so it also adds the two North/Bob rows (800 and 400). It computes 1200+800+600+400 = 3000 instead of 2100.

tasks.handCheck: Nine data rows, tested against Region=North AND Rep=Alice. r2 North/Alice 1200 IN. r3 North/Bob OUT (rep). r4 South/Alice OUT (region). r5 North/Alice 600 IN. r6 East/Carol OUT (both). r7 North/Bob OUT (rep). r8 South/Bob OUT (both). r9 North/Alice 300 IN. r10 East/Alice OUT (region). 1200 + 600 + 300 = 2100. All addends are integers below 2^53, so the sum is exact in binary64 regardless of accumulation order.

tasks.intent: In the order table in A1:C10, count how many rows have a Belopp that is STRICTLY greater than 1000 (a Belopp of exactly 1000 does not count) AND a Status of Skickad. Put the count in E2.
tasks.intentSv: Räkna hur många rader i ordertabellen A1:C10 som både har ett belopp strikt större än 1000 (exakt 1000 ska alltså inte räknas med) och status Skickad. Skriv antalet i E2.

distractor.why: It applies only the amount test and never looks at Status, so it also counts the two Makulerad rows over 1000 (2000 and 1100). It computes 6 instead of 4.

tasks.handCheck: Nine data rows against Belopp>1000 AND Status=Skickad. r2 1500 Skickad IN. r3 900 fails amount OUT. r4 2000 but Makulerad OUT. r5 1000 is NOT strictly greater than 1000 OUT. r6 1200 Skickad IN. r7 3000 Skickad IN. r8 1100 but Makulerad OUT. r9 800 Makulerad OUT (fails both). r10 2500 Skickad IN. Count = 4 (rows 2, 6, 7, 10). Row 5 is the boundary tooth: with ">=1000" the answer would be 5, so strict-versus-inclusive is measurable and is named in the intent.

tasks.intent: In the product list in A1:B9, add up the Units for every product whose code begins with the prefix WID- (the hyphen is part of the prefix). A code such as WIDGET, which starts with WID but has no hyphen, must NOT be included, and neither must a code that merely contains WID- somewhere later, such as TWID-500. Put the total in D2.

distractor.why: Dropping the hyphen from the pattern widens it: WID* also matches WIDGET, so the 25 units of WIDGET are added. It computes 50+40+20+25 = 135 instead of 110.

tasks.handCheck: Calcula anchors a wildcard pattern to the WHOLE cell text — xlookup_wildcard_match_recursive returns ti == text.len() when the pattern is exhausted — so "WID-*" means exactly 'starts with WID-'. r2 WID-100 matches -> 50. r3 GAD-200 no. r4 WID-205 matches -> 40. r5 WIDGET: pattern needs '-' at index 3, text has 'G' -> no match. r6 GAD-310 no. r7 WID-410 matches -> 20. r8 TWID-500: pattern needs 'W' at index 0, text has 'T', and the pattern has no leading star to skip it -> no match. r9 GAD-999 no. 50 + 40 + 20 = 110, exact in binary64.

tasks.intent: In the timesheet in A1:C10, work out the average Hours across the rows where the Employee is Anna AND the Department is Support, and round that average to 2 decimal places. Put the rounded average in E2.

distractor.why: The single-condition AVERAGEIF averages ALL of Anna's rows, including her two Sales rows (8 and 3). It computes (7+8+8+8+3)/5 = 34/5 = 6.8 instead of 7.67.

tasks.handCheck: Rows with Employee=Anna AND Department=Support: r2 (7), r6 (8), r8 (8). Excluded: Anna's Sales rows r4 (8) and r10 (3); Support rows belonging to someone else, r5 Cara (9) and r7 Ben (5); and r3 Ben/Sales (6), r9 Cara/Sales (4) which fail both. Sum = 23, count = 3, average = 23/3. In binary64 23.0/3.0 = 7.666666666666667. ROUND is implemented as (num * 10^digits).round() / 10^digits (fn_round, core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:4899-4920), so: 7.666666666666667 * 100 = 766.6666666666667, .round() = 767.0, 767.0/100.0 = 7.67. IEEE division is correctly rounded, so 767.0/100.0 is the nearest double to the real 7.67, which is bit-identical to what the literal 7.67 parses to. Confirmed by executing the exact double chain: the equality test 767/100 === 7.67 is true. Rounding direction is also load-bearing here: truncating to 2 decimals would give 7.66, so ROUND versus ROUNDDOWN is measurable.

tasks.intent: In the sales table in A1:C9, find the largest single Amount among the rows where the Region is West AND the Channel is Online. Rows in another region, and West rows sold through the Retail channel, must be ignored even when their Amount is bigger. Put the result in E2.

distractor.why: The one-condition version keeps every West row regardless of channel, so the West/Retail row of 6100 wins. It computes 6100 instead of 5300.

tasks.handCheck: Rows with Region=West AND Channel=Online: r2 (4200), r5 (5300), r7 (3100). max(4200, 5300, 3100) = 5300. The three decoys are deliberately larger: r3 East/Online 9500 is the global column maximum but the wrong region; r4 West/Retail 6100 is the maximum among West rows but the wrong channel; r6 North/Online 7000 is the maximum among Online rows but the wrong region. So MAX over the column (9500), MAXIFS on Region alone (6100) and MAXIFS on Channel alone (9500) all miss 5300. Every Amount is an integer, exact in binary64, and there are no ties.

tasks.intent: Column A holds SKUs, column B the product name and column C the price. Look up the SKU "SKU-107" with an exact match and return its price from column C. The match must be exact, so the similar code SKU-1070 in the list does not count as a match. Because SKU-107 itself is not in the list, the formula must return the text "Not found" (spelled exactly that way) instead of an error.

distractor.why: VLOOKUP has no if_not_found argument. With range_lookup FALSE the exact-match scan of the first column finds neither "SKU-107" nor an equal to it ("SKU-1070" is a different string), so fn_vlookup falls off the end of its loop and returns #N/A, not the text "Not found" the request asks for. The other reflex, =VLOOKUP("SKU-107",A2:C7,3,TRUE), is worse: the approximate branch keeps the last row whose key compares <= the target and so returns a neighbouring row's price silently instead of the fallback.

tasks.handCheck: Lookup array A2:A7 = SKU-100, SKU-101, SKU-102, SKU-103, SKU-104, SKU-1070. XLOOKUP's match_mode defaults to 0 (exact); exactness goes through Self::exact_lookup_equal -> excel_comparison_ordering, which compares text as text, so "SKU-107" is not equal to "SKU-1070" (different strings) nor to any other entry. found_index is None. args.len() is 4 > 3, so the None arm evaluates args[3], the literal "Not found", and returns it (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5540-5550 on the scan path, and the identical None arm at 5501-5507 on the lookup-cache fast path, so both spellings agree). Result = the text Not found.

tasks.intent: Column A lists the minimum quantity that starts each volume-discount tier and column B the discount percent for that tier. For an order of 75 units, return the discount percent for the band the order falls into, that is the row with the highest minimum quantity that is not above 75. 75 is not itself a listed threshold. Return the number as it stands in column B (10 meaning ten percent), not a fraction.

distractor.why: FALSE forces an exact match, but 75 is not one of the listed thresholds (0, 10, 50, 100, 250). fn_vlookup's exact branch scans the first column with exact_lookup_equal, matches nothing, and returns #N/A instead of 10. Reaching for exact match on a banded table is the standard reflex error; so is =XLOOKUP(75,A2:A6,B2:B6,"",1), which takes the next LARGER threshold, 100, and answers 15.

tasks.handCheck: Thresholds in A2:A6 are 0, 10, 50, 100, 250; returns in B2:B6 are 0, 5, 10, 15, 20. The reference passes -1 in the 5th positional slot, which the catalogue confirms is match_mode. fn_xlookup (evaluator.rs:5518-5523) dispatches match_mode -1 to xlookup_approx_smaller (evaluator.rs:5843-5877). That helper first tries an exact match: 75 is absent, so None. It then walks the whole array keeping the LARGEST number strictly less than 75: 0 (best), 10 (larger, best), 50 (larger, best), 100 (not < 75, skipped), 250 (skipped). best_index = 2 (0-based). return_array[2] = B4 = 10. Note the fast path is not taken here because it is gated on match_mode == 0 (evaluator.rs:5464), so only the scan path runs. Result = 10, an integer and therefore exact in binary floating point. The if_not_found "" is a positional placeholder needed to reach match_mode and never fires.

tasks.intent: The table has region names down column A and the quarter headings Q1 to Q4 across row 1, with the sales figures in B2:E5. Return the sales figure for the region East in quarter Q3, matching both the region name and the quarter heading exactly, so that the formula still finds the right cell if the quarter columns are reordered.

distractor.why: A hard-coded col_index_num counts columns from the left edge of table_array, so 3 is column C (Q2), not column D (Q3). fn_vlookup finds "East" in the first column at row 3 and returns row[2] = C4 = 210, not 190. It is a silent wrong number rather than an error, which is exactly why the wrong-column-index reflex survives review; it also cannot follow the heading if the quarter columns are reordered.

tasks.handCheck: MATCH("East",A2:A5,0): the array is North, South, East, West; fn_match's match_type 0 branch (evaluator.rs:8519-8538) returns i+1 for the first exact hit, so 3. MATCH("Q3",B1:E1,0): the array is Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, so 3. INDEX(B2:E5,3,3): the literal rectangle B2:E5 has rows=4, cols=4, and args.len()==3 so one_index is false and cols>1, giving flat_idx = row_num*cols + col_num = 2*4 + 2 = 10 (both indices are 0-based after the -1 at evaluator.rs:8403-8414). 10 < 16, so no #REF!. r = min_row + 10/4 = row(B2) + 2 = row 4; c = min_col + 10%4 = col B + 2 = col D. The cell is D4 = 190, an integer and exact in binary floating point.

tasks.intent: The staff list has the employee name in column A and the badge number in column B. Return the name of the employee whose badge number is exactly 4126. The answer sits to the LEFT of the badge column.
tasks.intentSv: Personallistan har namnen i kolumn A och bricknumren i kolumn B. Vilket namn hör till bricknummer 4126? Det ska vara en exakt träff, och namnet står till vänster om kolumnen med bricknummer.

distractor.why: VLOOKUP always searches the FIRST column of table_array, which here is the name column A. Its exact branch compares with exact_lookup_equal, which routes through excel_comparison_ordering; a number and a text value are different classes and are never equal (the same rule that makes ="1"=1 FALSE, evaluator.rs:2800-2816), so the number 4126 matches no name and the formula returns #N/A rather than Carla Nyman. VLOOKUP structurally cannot return a value to the left of its key.

tasks.handCheck: MATCH(4126,B2:B6,0): B2:B6 holds the numbers 4102, 4118, 4126, 4133, 4140; fn_match's exact branch (evaluator.rs:8519-8538) returns i+1 at the first exact_lookup_equal hit, which is the third entry, so 3. INDEX(A2:A6,3): A2:A6 is a literal rectangle with rows=5, cols=1, and args.len()==2 so one_index is true. Because cols<=1 the flat index is just row_num = 2 (0-based), well under rows*cols = 5, giving r = row(A2) + 2/1 = row 4 and c = col A + 2%1 = col A. That is A4 = "Carla Nyman" (evaluator.rs:8420-8431; the cols<=1 branch is the documented reading-order rule for a one-dimensional array). The four other rows - badges 4102, 4118, 4133, 4140 - are all excluded. Result = the text Carla Nyman.

tasks.intent: Column C holds the status of each task log entry. Return the position of the LAST entry whose status is Open, searching from the bottom of the list upward, counting the first data row (row 2) as position 1. Two entries are Open, and the later one is the answer. Return the position number itself, not the date or the task name.

distractor.why: MATCH has no search-direction argument (its third argument is match_type, not a direction), so fn_match always scans first to last and stops at the FIRST Open, C3, returning 2 instead of 4. The same wrong answer comes from writing =XMATCH("Open",C2:C6,0) and omitting the search_mode of -1, since fn_xmatch defaults search_mode to 1.

tasks.handCheck: C2:C6 is Closed, Open, Closed, Open, Closed at positions 1 to 5. fn_xmatch (evaluator.rs:14424-14452) builds its scan order from search_mode: -1 gives (0..len).rev(), i.e. 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 zero-based. match_mode 0 takes the exact branch. The lookup value "Open" is text so lookup_num is None, and the number-vs-number arm of the condition cannot fire; the else-if compares lookup_text to val.as_text(). i=4 is C6 "Closed", no match. i=3 is C5 "Open", match, and the function returns (i+1) = 4. Result = 4, an integer and exact. The first Open, at position 2, is the value that must be excluded - and it is exactly what the distractor returns, so the two are distinguishable.

tasks.intent: In H2, count the working days for the Site survey task in row 2: from its start date 2025-04-01 in B2 through its due date 2025-04-30 in C2, counting both of those days themselves, treating every Saturday and Sunday as a non-working day, and also skipping the public holidays listed in F2:F4.
tasks.intentSv: Räkna ut antalet arbetsdagar för uppgiften Site survey på rad 2: från startdatumet 2025-04-01 i B2 till och med slutdatumet 2025-04-30 i C2, där båda dagarna ska räknas med. Lördagar och söndagar är inte arbetsdagar, och helgdagarna som står i F2:F4 ska inte heller räknas. Skriv formeln i H2.

distractor.why: It drops the third argument, so the holiday list is never applied: it removes only the 8 weekend days and answers 22 instead of 20 (measured). The plainer wrong idiom =C2-B2 answers 29 (calendar days, and one short because it does not count the start day), and =C2-B2+1 answers 30.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently of the author. The grader seeds "2025-04-01" as a serial via seed_value -> date_serial::parse_date_string (core/calcula-format/src/ai/formula_verify.rs:192, core/engine/src/date_serial.rs:205), so B2 = 45748 and C2 = 45777; the inclusive window is all 30 days of April 2025. date_serial::weekday is ((serial-1) mod 7) with 0 = Sunday (date_serial.rs:136), so 45748 -> (45747 mod 7) = 2 = Tuesday and 45777 -> 3 = Wednesday. Saturdays inside: 04-05, 04-12, 04-19, 04-26; Sundays: 04-06, 04-13, 04-20, 04-27 -- 8 weekend days, leaving 30-8 = 22. Of the three holidays, F2 = 45765 = 2025-04-18 (WEEKDAY(...,2) = 5, Friday) and F3 = 45768 = 2025-04-21 (WEEKDAY(...,2) = 1, Monday) both lie inside the window on weekdays and each removes one day; F4 = 2025-05-01 lies outside and removes nothing. 22 - 2 = 20. CONFIRMED by running the fixture through the real grader (calcula_format::ai::formula_verify::evaluate_fixture over core/engine): reference = 20, =NETWORKDAYS(B2,C2) = 22, =C2-B2 = 29, =C2-B2+1 = 30, and the decoy row =NETWORKDAYS(B3,C3,F2:F4) = 15.

tasks.intent: In D2, work out how many COMPLETE years Anna Lind has been employed, from her hire date 2018-09-15 in B2 up to the as-of date 2025-06-30 in B7. Count only whole years: an anniversary that the as-of date has not yet reached does not count, so a part-year is dropped rather than rounded.

distractor.why: Subtracting calendar years ignores the month and day, so it counts the 2025 anniversary that has not happened yet and answers 7 instead of 6 (measured). The fixture is chosen so the two disagree: Anna's anniversary (15 September) falls AFTER the 30 June as-of date. Picking Bjorn Ek's row instead would have hidden the bug -- his March anniversary has already passed, and both formulas measure 5 there.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. B2 seeds to the serial for 2018-09-15 and B7 to 2025-06-30 (formula_verify::seed_value -> date_serial::parse_date_string). fn_datedif (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8214) converts both back with serial_to_date and calls date_serial::datedif_years (date_serial.rs:187), which is: years = ey - sy, then subtract one if em < sm or (em == sm and ed < sd). Here ey-sy = 2025-2018 = 7, and em = 6 is less than sm = 9, so one year is dropped: 6. The distractor is a plain calendar-year subtraction with no month test, so it keeps the 7. CONFIRMED against the real grader over this exact fixture: =DATEDIF(B2,B7,"Y") = 6, =YEAR(B7)-YEAR(B2) = 7, and the three decoy rows now measure 5 (B3), 9 (B4) and 4 (B5) -- all distinct from 6.

tasks.intent: In E2, count how many of the orders in B2:B8 were placed in March 2025, that is with an order date from 2025-03-01 to 2025-03-31 inclusive. Orders dated in March of any other year must not be counted.

distractor.why: The one-condition version tests the month only, so it also counts SO-103 dated 2024-03-19 and answers 4 instead of 3 (measured). March of a different year is exactly the row this fixture plants to catch it.

tasks.handCheck: Walk the seven dates: 2025-03-04 counts; 2025-02-28 is February, out; 2024-03-19 is March but 2024, out; 2025-03-17 counts; 2025-04-01 is one day past the window, out; 2025-03-31 counts (the inclusive upper bound); 2025-01-15 out. Three rows qualify. YEAR and MONTH are both on the array-lift allowlist (BuiltinFunction::Year at core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:3037 and ::Month at 3038, inside lifts_over_arrays at evaluator.rs:2945), so each returns an array over the range; the comparison yields a boolean array, TRUE coerces to 1 in EvalResult::as_number (evaluator.rs:641), and SUMPRODUCT sums the elementwise product. CONFIRMED against the real grader over this exact fixture: reference = 3, one-condition distractor = 4, the equivalent =COUNTIFS(B2:B8,">="&DATE(2025,3,1),B2:B8,"<="&DATE(2025,3,31)) = 3, and the trailing-*1 spelling =SUMPRODUCT((YEAR(B2:B8)=2025)*(MONTH(B2:B8)=3)*1) = 3.

tasks.intent: In E3, work out how many days there are from the invoice date of invoice F-2002 (2025-02-10, in B3) to its due date, where the due date is the last day of the month AFTER the invoice month. Report the difference as a plain whole number of days -- the due date minus the invoice date, with the invoice date itself counting as day zero -- not as a date.

distractor.why: Passing 0 months takes the end of the invoice's OWN month (2025-02-28) instead of the month after it, answering 18 instead of 49 (measured). Two further wrong idioms also fail on this fixture: =DAY(EOMONTH(B3,1)) answers 31 -- the length of March, not the distance to it -- and =EDATE(B3,1)-B3 answers 28, stepping one month rather than to a month end.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. seed_value turns "2025-02-10" into serial 45698 (grader-confirmed by evaluating =B3). fn_eomonth (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8172) converts to (2025,2), calls date_serial::add_months(2025,2,1,1) -> (2025,3), takes days_in_month(2025,3) = 31 and rebuilds the serial for 2025-03-31, which the grader reports as 45747 (evaluating =EOMONTH(B3,1)). 45747 - 45698 = 49. Cross-check without serials: 2025-02-10 to 2025-02-28 is 18 days (2025 is not a leap year, so February has 28), then 2025-02-28 to 2025-03-31 is 31 more; 18 + 31 = 49. CONFIRMED against the real grader over this exact fixture: reference = 49, =EOMONTH(B3,0)-B3 = 18, =DAY(EOMONTH(B3,1)) = 31, =EDATE(B3,1)-B3 = 28, and the inclusive misreading =EOMONTH(B3,1)-B3+1 = 50.

tasks.intent: In D2, count how many of the seven delivery dates in B2:B8 fall on a Saturday or a Sunday.

distractor.why: Omitting the return type leaves WEEKDAY on its default numbering (Sunday=1 .. Saturday=7), so >5 selects Friday and Saturday rather than Saturday and Sunday: it counts 2025-06-06 (Friday) and 2025-06-07 (Saturday) and answers 2 instead of 3 (measured). The fixture deliberately holds one Friday and two Sundays so the two conventions cannot agree.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently, then every value confirmed cell by cell against the real engine. fn_weekday (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8249) computes date_serial::weekday (0=Sunday..6=Saturday) and, for return_type 2, maps Sunday to 7 and every other day to its 0-based index, giving Monday=1..Sunday=7 (evaluator.rs:8258); so >5 is exactly Saturday or Sunday. Measured through the grader, one formula per cell: WEEKDAY(B2,2) = 1 (Mon), B3 = 5 (Fri), B4 = 6 (Sat), B5 = 7 (Sun), B6 = 3 (Wed), B7 = 7 (Sun), B8 = 3 (Wed). Three values exceed 5 -- B4, B5 and B7 -- so the count is 3. Under the default numbering (return_type 1, evaluator.rs:8257) those same seven days are 2, 6, 7, 1, 4, 1, 4, of which only two exceed 5. CONFIRMED against the real grader over this exact fixture: reference = 3, distractor = 2, and the equivalent =SUMPRODUCT((WEEKDAY(B2:B8,2)>=6)*1) = 3.

tasks.intent: Column B holds e-mail addresses. In E2, return only the domain part of the address in B3 — everything that comes after the @ sign, with the @ itself not included.

distractor.why: FIND returns the position OF the @ (5), so MID starts ON the @ instead of one character after it. Against this fixture it computes "@tallberg.com" — the right text with a stray leading @ — not "tallberg.com". The fix is FIND("@",B3)+1, which is exactly the off-by-one this task catches.

tasks.handCheck: AUDITOR RE-DERIVATION (author's handCheck ignored). B3 = "erik@tallberg.com". Character census: e,r,i,k = 4; @ = 1 (character 5); t,a,l,l,b,e,r,g = 8 (6-13); . = 1 (14); c,o,m = 3 (15-17). LEN(B3) = 17, and there is exactly one @, at character 5. TEXTAFTER(text, delimiter) with instance_num defaulted to 1 returns text[positions[0] + delimiter.len()..] — read at core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:11676 — i.e. everything strictly after the first @, which is characters 6..17 = "tallberg.com". Matches expectText. DISTRACTOR RE-DERIVATION: FIND("@",B3) = 5 (fn_find at core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:7766 returns a 1-based CHARACTER position via byte_offset_to_char_pos at line 154). LEN(B3) = 17. fn_mid (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5249) converts start 5 to a 0-based skip of 4, then takes 17 characters, so it yields "@tallberg.com" (13 characters). Different from the reference, so the task discriminates. OTHER WRONG ROUTES CHECKED: =TEXTAFTER(B3,".") = "com" (fails); =TEXTBEFORE(B3,"@") = "erik" (fails). Teeth: B2 and B4 end in @nordvind.se and B5 in @kvarnby.no, so no other row can produce "tallberg.com" — a misread row is visible. Result is pure text, so no floating-point question arises.

tasks.intent: Column B holds locations written as comma-separated parts, always ending with the country, but the NUMBER of parts varies from row to row — some rows are "City, Region, Country" and some carry an extra district part. In E2, return the country from B3 — that is, the part after the LAST comma, whichever comma that turns out to be — with any leading or trailing spaces removed.
tasks.intentSv: Kolumn B innehåller platser skrivna som kommaseparerade delar som alltid slutar med landet, men antalet delar varierar mellan raderna — vissa rader är "Stad, Region, Land" och vissa har ett extra stadsdelsled. Ge i E2 landet för B3, alltså den del som står efter det sista kommatecknet oavsett hur många kommatecken raden har, utan inledande eller avslutande blanksteg.

distractor.why: With no instance argument TEXTAFTER takes the FIRST comma, and it also keeps the space that follows it. Against this fixture it computes " Sentrum, Viken, Norway" — three parts glued together behind a leading space — instead of "Norway". A second tempting near-miss now fails too: because B3 carries THREE commas while the other rows carry two, the "count from the front" guess =TRIM(TEXTAFTER(B3,",",2)) returns "Viken, Norway", so only the negative instance -1 (count from the end) is right. The TRIM is separately load-bearing: without it the answer is " Norway" with a leading space.

tasks.handCheck: AUDITOR RE-DERIVATION (fixture changed by the audit; author's handCheck superseded). B3 = "Oslo, Sentrum, Viken, Norway". Character census: O,s,l,o = 1-4; "," = 5; space+S,e,n,t,r,u,m = 6-13; "," = 14; space+V,i,k,e,n = 15-20; "," = 21; space+N,o,r,w,a,y = 22-28. LEN = 28, and there are exactly THREE commas, at 5, 14 and 21. fn_textafter (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:11676) collects positions with match_indices, and for a negative instance uses idx = -instance-1 = 0 and pos = positions[positions.len()-1-idx] = positions[2] = the LAST comma; it returns text[pos + delimiter.len()..] = everything after character 21 = " Norway" (one space then six letters). fn_trim (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5125 — NOT 11611, which the author cited in error) does split_whitespace().join(" "), which strips both ends, giving "Norway". Matches expectText. DISTRACTOR RE-DERIVATION: =TEXTAFTER(B3,",") defaults to instance 1, positions[0] = 5, returns " Sentrum, Viken, Norway" — plainly different. SECOND NEAR-MISS RE-DERIVED: =TRIM(TEXTAFTER(B3,",",2)) takes positions[1] = 14, returns " Viken, Norway", trimmed to "Viken, Norway" — also different, which is the point of giving B3 three commas. Teeth: B2 -> Sweden, B4 -> Denmark, B5 -> Finland, none equal to "Norway". The answer text is pure ASCII even though B2 carries "Göteborg"; fn_textafter indexes by byte offsets taken from match_indices, which are always character boundaries, so the non-ASCII rows are safe and in any case are not the target row.

tasks.intent: Column B holds a comma-separated list of tags for each product; the tags are separated by a single comma with no spaces and there are no empty entries. In D2, count how many tags are listed for the Headlamp in B3. The answer is a whole number of tags, not a number of commas.

distractor.why: This counts the DELIMITERS, not the items. It computes 3 (the number of commas) instead of 4 (the number of tags); n commas separate n+1 tags, so the +1 is mandatory. On B3 it returns a plausible-looking 3, which is why the intent now says outright that the answer is a count of tags and not of commas.

tasks.handCheck: AUDITOR RE-DERIVATION (author's handCheck ignored, then found to agree). B3 = "outdoor,camping,winter,safety". Letter counts: outdoor = o,u,t,d,o,o,r = 7; camping = c,a,m,p,i,n,g = 7; winter = w,i,n,t,e,r = 6; safety = s,a,f,e,t,y = 6. Sum of letters = 7+7+6+6 = 26. Commas: three, between the four tags. LEN(B3) = 26 + 3 = 29. SUBSTITUTE(B3,",","") takes the three-argument branch of fn_substitute (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:7851), which is text.replace(old,new) over the WHOLE string, so every comma goes: "outdoorcampingwintersafety", LEN = 26 (fn_len at core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5077). 29 - 26 = 3 commas. Three commas separate four tags, so 3 + 1 = 4. The value is an exact small integer, so there is no floating-point ambiguity and no rounding decision to state. DISTRACTOR RE-DERIVATION: the same expression without the +1 is 29 - 26 = 3, which differs from 4. Teeth: B2 = 3 tags, B4 = 1, B5 = 2, B6 = 3 — no other row yields 4, so a misread row cannot pass. NOTE on the empty replacement: fn_substitute guards only old_text.is_empty(); an empty NEW text is ordinary and str::replace deletes the match, so the idiom is safe in this engine.

tasks.intent: Bin codes in column B are written as warehouse-aisle-shelf with a hyphen between the three blocks, and the blocks are NOT a fixed width. In E2, return only the middle block (the aisle) from B3 — the characters that lie between the first hyphen and the second hyphen, with neither hyphen included.

distractor.why: Fixed character positions read off the FIRST data row: in B2 ("WH1-A07-S3") characters 5 to 7 really are "A07", so the formula looks right on the row it was copied from. On B3 the aisle is four characters, so it computes "B11" — the aisle with its last character chopped off — instead of "B112". The blocks vary in width (A07, B112, C9, D4), so only a FIND-driven or TEXTBEFORE/TEXTAFTER formula works.

tasks.handCheck: AUDITOR RE-DERIVATION (author's handCheck ignored, then found to agree). B3 = "WH2-B112-S1", 11 characters: W(1) H(2) 2(3) -(4) B(5) 1(6) 1(7) 2(8) -(9) S(10) 1(11). Step 1: FIND("-",B3) with no start_num searches from offset 0 and reports the first hyphen; fn_find (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:7766) converts the byte hit through byte_offset_to_char_pos (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:154), which adds 1, so it returns 4. Step 2: FIND("-",B3,FIND("-",B3)+1) = FIND("-",B3,5). fn_find turns start_num 5 into the 0-based character offset 4, maps that to byte offset 4 via char_to_byte_offset, searches "B112-S1", finds the hyphen 4 bytes in, and reports byte_offset_to_char_pos(text, 8) = 9. Step 3: start = FIND+1 = 5; length = 9 - 4 - 1 = 4. Step 4: fn_mid (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5249) skips start-1 = 4 characters and takes 4, giving characters 5,6,7,8 = "B112". Matches expectText. DISTRACTOR RE-DERIVATION: MID(B3,5,3) skips 4 and takes 3 = characters 5,6,7 = "B11", which is NOT "B112". Sanity check that the distractor is genuinely tempting rather than absurd: on B2 it gives characters 5,6,7 of "WH1-A07-S3" = "A07", the correct aisle for that row, which is exactly how a fixed-position formula gets written in the first place. The modern spelling =TEXTBEFORE(TEXTAFTER(B3,"-"),"-") is an equally correct answer: TEXTAFTER gives "B112-S1" and TEXTBEFORE then gives "B112". The answer is alphanumeric so it cannot be coerced to a number. Teeth: aisle widths are 3 (row 2), 4 (row 3), 2 (row 4) and 2 (row 5), and no row other than B3 yields "B112".

tasks.intent: Cell B2 holds a whole pasted partner list in one cell: records are separated by a vertical bar (|), and inside a record the company name and the city are separated by " - " (a space, a hyphen, and a space). A company name may itself contain a hyphen with no spaces around it, and that hyphen must be kept as part of the name. In D2, split B2 so that the result spills as one row per record and two columns — the company first, then the city — leaving D2 itself holding the first company name.

distractor.why: It splits on a bare hyphen instead of on the three-character " - ", so it also cuts the company name in half at the hyphen inside the name. The first record becomes three fields — "Nord", "Vind AB " and " Stockholm" — so the spill is 3 columns wide and the anchor cell D2 holds "Nord" instead of "Nord-Vind AB". Recognising that the delimiter is a multi-character string, not a single punctuation mark, is exactly what this task tests.

tasks.handCheck: AUDITOR RE-DERIVATION (fixture delimiter changed by the audit; recomputed from scratch). B2 = "Nord-Vind AB - Stockholm|Tallberg AB - Oslo". fn_textsplit (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:11616) takes args (text, col_delimiter, row_delimiter), and when a row delimiter is present it splits by ROWS FIRST: text.split("|") gives exactly two records, "Nord-Vind AB - Stockholm" and "Tallberg AB - Oslo" (there is one bar and it is not adjacent to another, so no empty record appears). Each record is then split on the column delimiter " - ": record 1 contains one occurrence of space-hyphen-space, between "AB" and "Stockholm" — the hyphen inside "Nord-Vind" has no surrounding spaces so it is not a match — giving ["Nord-Vind AB", "Stockholm"]; record 2 gives ["Tallberg AB", "Oslo"]. The result is EvalResult::Array of two Arrays of two. spill_dimensions (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:842) reads a nested array as (outer_len, inner_len) = (2,2), so the spill is 2 rows by 2 columns. to_spill_values (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:860) emits offset (0,0) for the first element of the first row, so D2 = "Nord-Vind AB", E2 = "Stockholm", D3 = "Tallberg AB", E3 = "Oslo". Matches expectText at the anchor. DISTRACTOR RE-DERIVATION: with col_delimiter "-", record 1 splits into ["Nord", "Vind AB ", " Stockholm"] and record 2 into ["Tallberg AB ", " Oslo"]; the anchor becomes "Nord", which is different. Row-delimiter guard checked: fn_textsplit treats the row delimiter as absent only when it is FALSE, 0, or an empty string — "|" is a non-empty Text, so the two-dimensional branch is taken. Spill region D2:E3 is empty and clear of the fixture, which occupies A1:B4. Teeth: B3 and B4 open with different companies (Kvarn-By AB, Ost-Vik AB), each carrying its own internal hyphen, so neither a misread row nor a bare-hyphen split can land on "Nord-Vind AB".

tasks.intent: In D2, join every email address in B2:B6 into one single text value, in the order they appear from top to bottom, separated by a comma and a space, and leave out the people who have no email address (their email cell is empty).
tasks.intentSv: Skriv i D2 en enda text som slår ihop alla e-postadresser i B2:B6, uppifrån och ned, åtskilda med kommatecken och mellanslag, och hoppa över de personer som saknar e-postadress.

distractor.why: ignore_empty=FALSE keeps the two absent cells as empty fields, so it computes "anna@acme.com, , carla@acme.com, , elin@acme.com" (five fields, doubled delimiters) instead of the three real addresses. I traced this through the code rather than assuming: core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:11555-11558, the `None =>` arm of the direct range walk, pushes `String::new()` for a missing cell exactly when `!ignore_empty`. The TRUE/FALSE choice is the only difference between reference and distractor, which is what the task measures.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. `TRUE` is lexed as a boolean literal, not a function call (core/parser/src/lexer.rs:463 `"TRUE" => Token::Boolean(true)`), and fn_textjoin reads arg[1] as `EvalResult::Boolean(b) => b` (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:9649-9650), so ignore_empty is genuinely true. The range arm walks B2:B6 top to bottom (evaluator.rs:11531-11556): B2 is CellValue::Text("anna@acme.com"), pushed because the string is non-empty; B3 has no cell at all, so the `None` arm pushes nothing because ignore_empty is true; B4 pushed; B5 None, skipped; B6 pushed. parts = [anna@acme.com, carla@acme.com, elin@acme.com], joined with ", " = two delimiters: 13 + 2 + 14 + 2 + 13 = 44 characters, "anna@acme.com, carla@acme.com, elin@acme.com". Matches the author's expectText exactly.

tasks.intent: In E2, build the shipping label for the order in row 3: the text ORD- followed immediately by the order number in A3, padded with leading zeros so the number part is exactly 5 digits long.

distractor.why: Concatenating the raw number gives "ORD-8": eval_concat renders the number 8 as the text "8" with no padding, so the label is 5 characters instead of 9 and the zero padding the intent asks for never happens. I confirmed the distractor and the reference differ; the task discriminates.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. A3 is typed "8", which the loader stores as the number 8. fn_text (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5297) evaluates arg[0], sees a non-empty format string, and routes `value.as_number()` = Some(8.0) into `custom_format::format_custom_value(8.0, "00000", &self.locale)` (evaluator.rs:5330-5333). "00000" is five zero digit-placeholders; the engine's own test pins this behaviour at core/engine/src/custom_format.rs:2072-2075, `format_custom_value(5.0, "000", &LocaleSettings::invariant())` == "005". By the same rule 8 with five placeholders yields "00008". The format contains no comma group token and no decimal point, so the `&self.locale` argument cannot change the result — the answer is identical on an sv-SE build and an invariant one. Then "ORD-" & "00008" = "ORD-00008", 9 characters. Extra robustness I checked that the author did not: even if the loader stored A3 as the TEXT "8", `as_number` coerces text through number_text::parse (evaluator.rs:650-654) and still returns 8.0, so the expectation holds under either storage decision.

tasks.intent: In E2, build the account code for the person in row 2: the department name from C2 in capital letters, then a hyphen with no spaces around it, then the last name from B2 in capital letters.

distractor.why: It concatenates the cells as typed, computing "sales-Nilsson": the department stays lowercase and the surname keeps only its initial capital, so neither half is in capital letters. The fixture is deliberately mixed-case — every department is lowercase and every surname is capitalised — so omitting UPPER cannot accidentally produce the right string for any row.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. C2 holds the text "sales"; UPPER maps it to "SALES" (fn_upper, dispatched at core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:3350). B2 holds "Nilsson"; UPPER gives "NILSSON". Concat is left-associative: ("SALES" & "-") = "SALES-", then & "NILSSON" = "SALES-NILSSON", 5 + 1 + 7 = 13 characters. Matches expectText. Note the alternative spelling =UPPER(C2&"-"&B2) yields the identical string and is equally correct, since the hyphen is case-invariant.

tasks.intent: Cell A3 was pasted in from another system: it is written all in capital letters and has two spaces between the words. In D2, write a cleaned-up copy of A3 that has a single space between the words and only the first letter of each word capitalized.

distractor.why: PROPER only changes letter case; its else-branch pushes every non-alphanumeric character through untouched (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:7939-7942). It therefore computes "Maria  Lund" with both spaces still in the middle, 11 characters instead of 10. Dropping TRIM is the single most likely near-miss, and the intent names the single-space requirement explicitly.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently by reading both implementations. A3 holds "MARIA  LUND" — two spaces. fn_trim (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5125-5134) is `text.split_whitespace().collect::<Vec<&str>>().join(" ")`, which drops empty segments and rejoins with exactly one space, so TRIM gives "MARIA LUND". fn_proper (evaluator.rs:7930-7945) walks characters with a capitalize_next flag: 'M' is alphanumeric and the flag is set, so it is upper-cased and the flag clears; 'A','R','I','A' are lower-cased to "aria"; the single space is not alphanumeric so it is pushed as-is and re-arms the flag; 'L' is upper-cased; 'U','N','D' lower-cased. Result "Maria Lund", 10 characters. Matches expectText. Nesting order does not matter here: TRIM(PROPER(A3)) = TRIM("Maria  Lund") = "Maria Lund" as well, so both spellings are correct.

tasks.intent: In D2, write the product code from A2 followed by enough dots for the whole result to be exactly 8 characters long.

distractor.why: A fixed repeat count ignores how long the code already is, computing "AX12........" — four code characters plus eight dots, 12 characters instead of 8. The repeat count has to be 8 minus the code's own length, which is what LEN supplies.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. A2 holds the text "AX12" (it begins with letters, so it cannot be read as a number). LEN("AX12") = 4, so the second argument evaluates to 8 - 4 = 4. fn_rept (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5272-5295) takes `as_number()` on that argument, rejects negatives, then casts with `n as usize` — 4.0 casts to 4 with no rounding question, since 8 and 4 are both exactly representable and their difference is exact in binary floating point. REPT(".", 4) = ".".repeat(4) = "....". Concat then gives "AX12" & "...." = "AX12....", 4 + 4 = exactly 8 characters. Matches expectText.

tasks.intent: Column C should show a running (cumulative) total of the Amount in column B, starting at the first data row, row 2. Write the formula for cell C7 — the total of B2 down through B7 — as a fill-down formula: the sum must always begin at row 2 no matter which row of column C it is copied into, and it must end at the formula's own row. The amount on row 8 belongs to a later week and must not be counted.
tasks.intentSv: Kolumn C ska visa en löpande summa av beloppen i kolumn B, räknat från och med rad 2. Skriv formeln för cell C7, alltså summan av B2 till och med B7. Formeln ska gå att kopiera nedåt i hela kolumnen utan att startraden flyttas, så rad 2 måste ligga fast medan slutraden följer med. Beloppet på rad 8 ska inte räknas med.

distractor.why: Anchoring BOTH endpoints is the over-application of the '$ makes fill-down work' idiom, and it also happens to be what a model produces when it reads 'Amount column' as the whole column rather than 'up to my own row'. It sweeps B2:B8 and answers 120+80+150+60+200+90+110 = 810 instead of 700, because it swallows week 7 (110), which the intent explicitly excludes. It is additionally wrong as a fill-down formula: copied to any row it returns the same 810, so the column shows a flat grand total rather than a rising cumulative curve. Only a half-anchored range ($B$2 fixed, B7 relative) both stops at the current row and keeps the window expanding.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently of the author. B2:B7 = 120, 80, 150, 60, 200, 90. 120+80 = 200; 200+150 = 350; 350+60 = 410; 410+200 = 610; 610+90 = 700. So C7 = 700. Every addend is a small integer, so the sum is exact in binary floating point and no rounding decision is needed. Row 8 (110) is outside the range: the distractor =SUM($B$2:$B$8) reaches it and answers 700+110 = 810, so 810 != 700 and the task discriminates at the target cell itself. SUM over a literal range is verified index-parallel and total-only in fn_sum; no blanks or text sit inside B2:B7, so there is no blank-handling ambiguity to state.

tasks.intent: Column C should show how much the water-meter Reading in column B changed from the immediately preceding month. Write the formula for cell C5 (April): April's reading minus March's reading. It is a plain difference in reading units, not a percentage and not an absolute value, so a month where the reading fell must come out negative. The formula is meant to be filled down column C, so it must always look one row up rather than back at a fixed month.

distractor.why: Anchoring the second operand turns a period-over-period change into a change-since-January: it computes 1150 - 1000 = 150 instead of 1150 - 1180 = -30. It even gets the sign wrong, so the reading looks like it rose when it actually fell. This is the exact mirror of the running-total idiom — here the anchor must NOT be there, and a model that has learned '$ makes fill-down work' over-applies it.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently of the author. B5 (April) = 1150, B4 (March) = 1180. 1150 - 1180 = -30. Both operands are integers well inside the exactly-representable range, so the difference is exact in binary floating point; no rounding decision is in play. The sign is load-bearing: April is the one month in the fixture where the reading FELL, so a formula that took an absolute value would answer +30 and a formula that subtracted in the other direction (=B4-B5) would also answer +30. Rows below the target (May 1300, June 1360) must not enter the answer, and January (1000) must not either — the named distractor =B5-$B$2 reaches January and answers 1150-1000 = 150, which is 180 away from the correct value and carries the opposite sign.

tasks.intent: A2:B8 is a bank ledger of seven transactions in date order, with deposits entered as positive amounts and withdrawals as negative ones; row 9 is a Total row and is not a transaction. The account's opening balance, before the first transaction, was 1000. In cell D2 write ONE formula that spills seven running balances down D2:D8 — each one the opening balance plus every transaction up to and including that row. The first spilled result is therefore the opening balance plus the first transaction, 1000 + (-150). Do not scan the Total row, and do not emit the opening balance itself as an extra eighth output row.

distractor.why: The expanding-window SUM is the cell-by-cell way to write a running total and the idiom a small model reaches for first, but it is wrong twice over here. It silently drops the opening balance, so at D2 it evaluates to -150 instead of 850; and it is not a spilling formula at all, so it fills one cell where the intent demands a single formula covering seven. A model that answers with the familiar anchored SUM gets both the number and the shape wrong.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently of the author, against the engine source rather than against Excel intuition. SCAN's contract: core/parser/src/ast.rs:2057 gives 'SCAN(initial_value, array, lambda)', so 1000 is the init, B2:B8 the array, the LAMBDA third — argument order in the reference matches. fn_scan (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:9461-9494) seeds the accumulator with the init and pushes ONE result per item AFTER folding, so the init is NOT prepended and seven inputs give exactly seven outputs. Confirmed live by the shipped test at app/extensions/TestRunner/lib/suites/lambda.ts:185-200, which writes =SCAN(0, A1:A3, LAMBDA(acc, x, acc+x)) over 1/2/3 and asserts three spilled cells reading 1, 3, 6 — same lambda shape, init not emitted. Shape: B2:B8 is seven cells; a flat EvalResult::Array yields (n, 1) per spill_dimensions at core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:842, so the spill is 7 rows x 1 col into D2:D8. Anchor value: 1000 + (-150) = 850. Full spill for the record: 850, 1150, 1075, 1575, 1355, 1500, 1100 (850+300=1150; 1150-75=1075; 1075+500=1575; 1575-220=1355; 1355+145=1500; 1500-400=1100). Cross-check on the Total row: B9 = -150+300-75+500-220+145-400 = 100, and 1000+100 = 1100, which matches the last spilled balance, so the ledger is internally consistent. Every intermediate is an integer, exact in binary floating point.

tasks.intent: Column C should show, for each row, the cumulative Units sold so far divided by the grand total of all Units in the table — a decimal fraction between 0 and 1, not a percentage and with no rounding applied. Write the formula for cell C6: the running total of B2 through B6 divided by the total of the whole data range B2:B9. It is meant to be filled down column C, so the running total must always start at row 2 and end at the formula's own row, while the divisor must always stay the full range B2:B9.

distractor.why: This is the plain share-of-total formula, and it is what a model produces when it latches onto 'divided by the grand total' and drops the word 'cumulative'. It answers Friday's own 200 / 800 = 0.25 instead of the running 600 / 800 = 0.75. The numerator has to be an expanding SUM from row 2, not the single current cell — that expanding numerator against a fixed divisor is the entire point of the task, and this distractor gets the divisor right and the numerator wrong, so it isolates exactly the skill under test.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently of the author. Grand total B2:B9 = 100+50+150+100+200+50+100+50: 100+50=150, +150=300, +100=400, +200=600, +50=650, +100=750, +50=800. Divisor = 800. Running total B2:B6 = 100+50+150+100+200: 100+50=150, +150=300, +100=400, +200=600. Numerator = 600. 600/800 = 0.75. Both 600 and 800 are exactly representable in binary floating point and IEEE-754 division is correctly rounded, so the quotient is exactly 0.75 — the one value in this family that could have been a floating-point trap and is not, which is why the fixture uses these round numbers. No rounding function is needed or wanted, and the intent says so. Rows 7, 8 and 9 (50, 100, 50) are excluded from the numerator but required in the divisor: a formula that swept B2:B9 in both places answers 800/800 = 1.0, and the named distractor =B6/SUM($B$2:$B$9) answers 200/800 = 0.25. Both differ from 0.75.

tasks.intent: Column C should show a running total per region: for each row, the sum of Amount for that row's own Region, counting only rows from the first data row (row 2) down to and including the formula's own row. Write the formula for cell C7, which is a South row, so the answer covers the South amounts on rows 2 through 7 only. It is meant to be filled down column C, so the scanned range must always start at row 2 and end at the formula's own row; the South amount on row 8 and the North amount on row 9 come later and must not be counted. Match the region by reading it from the formula's own row rather than typing the word South into the formula, so the same formula works on a North row too.

distractor.why: This is the ordinary sum-by-region formula and the thing a model writes when it hears 'sum the Amount for this row's Region' without carrying the word 'running' through to the range. Both ranges are pinned to the full table, so it matches every South row in the sheet — 50 + 300 + 25 + 400 = 775 — instead of stopping at the formula's own row for 375. It is also flat as a fill-down formula: every South row in column C would show the same 775, so the column reports a category total rather than a running one. Only absolute STARTS with relative ENDS ($A$2:A7 and $B$2:B7) make the two windows grow together as the formula moves down.

tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently of the author. The reference's criteria range $A$2:A7 covers rows 2-7 and its sum range $B$2:B7 covers the same six rows; fn_sumif (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:6421-6455) walks the criteria values by index and adds the sum value at the SAME index, so the two six-cell ranges line up one-to-one and no Excel-style range resizing is involved. Criteria A7 is evaluated first (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:6436) and resolves to the text 'South', an exact-match criterion. South rows within rows 2-7: row 3 = 50, row 5 = 300, row 7 = 25. 50+300 = 350; 350+25 = 375. So C7 = 375. All integers, exact in binary floating point. Excluded and why: the North rows 2 (100), 4 (200) and 6 (150) fail the criteria; row 8 (South, 400) and row 9 (North, 60) fall outside the range end. The named distractor =SUMIF($A$2:$A$9,A7,$B$2:$B$9) reaches row 8 and answers 50+300+25+400 = 775; a formula that got the range right but hard-coded the wrong region would answer 100+200+150 = 450 for North over rows 2-7. Both differ from 375.

tasks.intent: In E2, return the third largest order amount from the seven amounts in C2:C8. All seven amounts are different, so there are no ties to break.

distractor.why: SMALL counts up from the bottom, so it returns the THIRD SMALLEST amount, 4200, not the third largest 7500. LARGE and SMALL are the classic swapped pair; the fixture is built so the two answers are far apart (4200 vs 7500) and neither coincides with any other plausible reading.

tasks.handCheck: Amounts in C2:C8 = 4200, 7500, 3100, 9800, 6400, 2500, 8600 (seven distinct integers). Sorted descending: 9800 (1st), 8600 (2nd), 7500 (3rd), 6400 (4th), 4200 (5th), 3100 (6th), 2500 (7th). The 3rd entry is 7500, so LARGE(C2:C8,3) = 7500 exactly (integer, exact in binary floating point). Rows that the answer must exclude: C5 (9800) and C8 (8600) are larger and must NOT be returned; C6/C2/C4/C7 are smaller and must not be returned either. Sorted ascending the list is 2500, 3100, 4200, 6400, 7500, 8600, 9800, so the distractor SMALL(...,3) = 4200 != 7500.

tasks.intent: In D4, return the rank of Cecilia's sales figure (the amount in B4) within all seven sales figures in B2:B8, where the LARGEST amount is rank 1. Two people are tied on 9000, and tied amounts must both receive the same rank - the better (lower) one - not an averaged rank.

distractor.why: A non-zero order argument switches RANK.EQ to ASCENDING ranking (smallest = rank 1). Models frequently pass 1 believing it means 'rank 1 is the top'. Counting values strictly LESS than 9000 gives 7500, 5000, 6800 = 3, so the distractor returns 4 instead of 3.

tasks.handCheck: B2:B8 = 12000, 9000, 9000, 7500, 15000, 5000, 6800. Target value is B4 = 9000. Descending RANK.EQ = (count of values strictly greater than 9000) + 1. Strictly greater: 12000 and 15000 = 2 values. Rank = 2 + 1 = 3. This matches the implementation at core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8856 fn_rank, which with order 0 computes numbers.iter().filter(|n| n > number).count() + 1. Tie rule check: Bertil (B3) also holds 9000 and also gets 3, and the next distinct amount 7500 gets rank 5 - competition ranking, which is what the intent states. An averaged (RANK.AVG) reading would give 3.5 and a descending-order-flag mistake gives 4, so the stated tie rule and the stated direction are both load-bearing and both named in the intent. Ascending check for the distractor: values below 9000 are 7500, 5000, 6800 = 3, so 3 + 1 = 4 != 3.

tasks.intent: In E2, return the largest amount in C2:C8, counting only the rows whose region in B2:B8 is Nord.
tasks.intentSv: Skriv i E2 det högsta beloppet i C2:C8, men bara för de rader där regionen i B2:B8 är Nord.

distractor.why: Dropping the condition returns the overall maximum, 74000, which belongs to David in the Syd region - a row the answer must exclude. B2:B7 is a 6-row, 1-column Range, so eval_range materializes it positionally and, crucially, absent cells become EvalResult::Blank rather than Number(0.0) (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:1899-1917 and the comment above it). Teeth: Bruno's B3 = 0 MUST be excluded - it is the row that separates a real blank test from a zero test - and the three genuine entries 38, 35 and 42 must be excluded as well, so four of the six cells in the range are excluded by the correct answer.

tasks.intent: Cell D2 must answer TRUE or FALSE to one question: does the name Farid appear anywhere in the name list A2:A6? Find that name's position in the list with an exact match, then report whether a position was found - TRUE when the name is on the roster, FALSE when it is not. distractor.why: The same idiom with the test inverted. MATCH still returns #N/A, and fn_iserror (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:5391-5397) answers Boolean(result.is_error()) = TRUE, so D2 says TRUE where FALSE is required. ISERROR is the exact inverse of the question in BOTH directions - TRUE for a name that is absent, FALSE for one that is present - so it is never right for either case, not merely unlucky on this fixture. tasks.handCheck: Re-derived independently. fn_match (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8499) with match_type 0 takes the exact branch (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8519-8538) and walks A2:A6 = Anna, Bruno, Clara, Dinesh, Elena. tasks.intent: In E2, use one formula to list the rep names from A2:A9 for every row where the Region in column B is North AND the Amount in column C is strictly greater than 200 (an amount of exactly 200 does not qualify). Keep the rows in their original sheet order and let the result spill down.

Row-by-row: Anna 1*0=0 EXCLUDED (120 <= 200); Hanna 1*0=0 EXCLUDED (200 is not > 200); Bjorn 0*1=0 EXCLUDED (South); Carl 1*1=1 KEPT; Diana 0*1=0 EXCLUDED (West); Erik 1*1=1 KEPT; Fatima 0*0=0 EXCLUDED; Gustav 1*1=1 KEPT. FILTER preserves sheet order and, because cols==1, returns a FLAT array (evaluator.rs:9765-9767): {"Carl";"Erik";"Gustav"} = 3 rows x 1 column. Anchor E2 = "Carl". Pure text selection, no arithmetic, so the value is exact.

tasks.intent: In D2, use one formula that takes the product names in A2:A8, removes the duplicates so each name is kept once, and returns them sorted in descending alphabetical order (Z to A). Let the result spill down.

distractor.why: SORT's sort_order argument defaults to 1 = ascending when it is omitted (fn_sort, evaluator.rs:9830-9834), so this returns Apple, Banana, Cherry, Pear and the anchor D2 reads "Apple" instead of "Pear". The intent explicitly says Z to A, so the descending flag is pinned by the wording.

tasks.handCheck: UNIQUE(A2:A8) keeps the FIRST occurrence of each value in order of appearance (unique_vectors, evaluator.rs:10111-10150): Pear (row2), Apple (row3), Cherry (row5), Banana (row7). Rows 4, 6 and 8 are the duplicates the answer must EXCLUDE. That is 4 values and cols==1, so UNIQUE returns a flat array. SORT then re-reads that value's shape through get_range_dimensions' non-rectangle branch (evaluator.rs:8488-8495) as 4 rows x 1 column, so sort_index 1 is within bounds. Text sorts on the UPPERCASED string key (compare_eval_results, evaluator.rs:9940) and sort_order -1 reverses the comparison: ascending is APPLE < BANANA < CHERRY < PEAR, so descending is PEAR, CHERRY, BANANA, APPLE. Original casing survives because the sort only reorders the stored EvalResults. Spill = 4 rows x 1 column, anchor D2 = "Pear".

tasks.intent: In E2, use one formula that returns just the driver names from A2:A6 as a single column of five names (no other columns), arranged from the most Miles to the fewest Miles using the Miles values in C2:C6. Do not include the header row. Let the result spill down.

distractor.why: With sort_order1 omitted, SORTBY's argument walk falls to its trailing else and defaults the order to 1 = ascending (fn_sortby, evaluator.rs:9985-9990), so the drivers come back fewest-miles-first: Petra(60), Ivan(71), Omar(82), Quinn(88), Nadia(95). The anchor E2 would read "Petra" instead of "Nadia". The intent says most miles first, so the -1 is pinned by the wording. Two further wrong forms also fail on the anchor: including the header row, =SORTBY(A1:A6,C1:C6,-1), puts the TEXT "Miles" ahead of every number under a reversed sort (Text is sort class 1, Number class 0, evaluator.rs:9939-9940) and the anchor reads "Driver"; and sorting by the decoy Stops column, =SORTBY(A2:A6,B2:B6,-1), puts Omar(15 stops) first.

tasks.handCheck: SORTBY sorts the rows of A2:A6 by the parallel key vector C2:C6 with order -1. fn_sortby's argument walk reads args[1] as by_array1 (5 values, matching rows=5) and args[2] as a number, so order = -1 (evaluator.rs:9968-9990). The five Miles values are Ivan 71, Nadia 95, Omar 82, Petra 60, Quinn 88. compare_eval_results puts Numbers in class 0 and compares them numerically (evaluator.rs:9939); order -1 reverses that comparison. Descending: 95 Nadia, 88 Quinn, 82 Omar, 71 Ivan, 60 Petra. All five keys are distinct integers, so the sort is total and no tie rule can be reached. Because the sorted array is A2:A6 only, cols==1 and the result is a flat 5-row column of NAMES, not miles. Spill = 5 rows x 1 column, anchor E2 = "Nadia". The fixture row that the answer must EXCLUDE is header row 1: including it drags the text "Miles" into the key vector, where it outranks every number under a descending sort and makes the anchor "Driver". Column B (Stops) is a decoy key whose descending order starts with Omar, not Nadia.

tasks.intent: In D2, use one formula to build a SINGLE column of shift IDs: produce as many numbers as the count in B2, starting at the First shift ID in B3 (not the Previous first ID in B5, which must be ignored) and increasing by the step in B4 for each following number. Let the result spill down.

distractor.why: SEQUENCE's SECOND argument is `columns`, not `start` (signature SEQUENCE(rows, [columns], [start], [step]), catalogue entry at core/parser/src/ast.rs:2473). Omitting the columns argument makes the engine read rows=B2=6, columns=B3=20, start=B4=5 and step=1 (fn_sequence, evaluator.rs:10156-10190), producing a 6x20 block of 120 cells running 5..124 whose anchor is 5, not 20 -- wrong value AND wrong shape. A second wrong form fails on the anchor too: reading the start from the decoy B5 gives =SEQUENCE(B2,1,B5,B4) = 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, whose anchor is 15.

tasks.handCheck: SEQUENCE(rows=B2=6, columns=1, start=B3=20, step=B4=5). fn_sequence reads the four arguments positionally (evaluator.rs:10159-10186), rejects the 1x1 shortcut because seq_rows is 6, then takes the seq_cols==1 branch and emits a flat column, adding the step AFTER pushing each value (evaluator.rs:10204-10211): 20, then 20+5=25, 25+5=30, 30+5=35, 35+5=40, 40+5=45. Six values. Every one is a small integer, exactly representable in binary floating point, and 5 is exact too, so no rounding decision exists. Spill = 6 rows x 1 column, anchor D2 = 20. Row 5 (Previous first ID = 15) is the decoy the answer must EXCLUDE: using B5 as the start would make the anchor 15 instead of 20.

tasks.intent: In E2, use one formula to list the ticket IDs from A2:A7 that are both High priority (column B) and Open (column C). If no ticket matches both conditions, the formula must return the text None instead of an error.

distractor.why: The conditions are right but the if_empty argument is missing, so with zero matching rows fn_sequence's sibling fn_filter falls past the args.len() >= 3 test and returns CellError::Value -- a literal #VALUE! error (evaluator.rs:9756-9762) -- instead of the text "None" the intent requires. A second trap fails from the other side: the one-condition version =FILTER(A2:A7,B2:B7="High","None") finds two High rows and spills {"T-102";"T-105"}, so it never reaches the fallback at all and its anchor reads "T-102".

tasks.handCheck: Evaluate (Priority="High") * (Status="Open") for rows 2-7. T-101: Low=0, Open=1 -> 0. T-102: High=1, Closed=0 -> 0. T-103: Low=0, Closed=0 -> 0. T-104: Medium=0, Open=1 -> 0. T-105: High=1, Closed=0 -> 0. T-106: Medium=0, Open=1 -> 0. The include vector is a 6x1 array of zeros, which get_range_dimensions measures from the VALUE (evaluator.rs:8488-8495) as inc_rows=6, inc_cols=1, matching rows=6, so FILTER takes the filter_by_row branch. Every product is 0, no row is truthy, result_rows is empty, and fn_filter evaluates the third argument because args.len() >= 3 (evaluator.rs:9756-9760), returning the scalar Text "None". The fixture deliberately contains High tickets (T-102, T-105) and Open tickets (T-101, T-104, T-106) but no ticket that is both, so ONLY the two-condition form reaches the fallback. A scalar Text does not spill: spill_dimensions answers (1,1) for any non-Array (evaluator.rs:842-856), so spills=false. Anchor E2 = "None".

tasks.intent: In D2, work out the average of the five order amounts in B2:B6 (the Total row in row 7 is not an order and must be left out), then round that average to the NEAREST multiple of 5 — nearest in either direction, not always upward.

distractor.why: CEILING(number, significance) rounds UP to a multiple of 5 rather than to the nearest one. The average is 1221.4, which is nearer 1220 than 1225, so CEILING returns 1225 instead of 1220. Two further traps the fixture now catches: =ROUND(AVERAGE(B2:B6),0) rounds to the nearest whole number and returns 1221; =MROUND(AVERAGE(B2:B7),5) swallows the Total row (12214/6 = 2035.667) and returns 2035.

tasks.handCheck: B2:B6 = 1240 + 985 + 1310 + 1122 + 1450. 1240+985=2225; +1310=3535; +1122=4657; +1450=6107. AVERAGE = 6107/5 = 1221.4. fn_mround (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:16345) computes (number/multiple).round()*multiple = (1221.4/5).round()*5 = (244.28).round()*5 = 244*5 = 1220, an exact integer in binary floating point. Distances confirm the direction: 1221.4 - 1220 = 1.4 versus 1225 - 1221.4 = 3.6, so the nearest multiple of 5 is BELOW. B7 evaluates to 6107 and lies outside the B2:B6 range.

tasks.intent: In D2, report the median number of resolution hours across the tickets in B2:B8 — the middle value, and with an even count of numbers the average of the two middle values. Ticket T-06 is still open and has no hours logged, so its empty cell is not part of the population and must not be counted as a zero.

A second failure mode the fixture catches: treating the empty B7 as a zero gives the sorted list 0,2,3,4,6,9,71 — an odd count of seven — with a median of 4.

tasks.handCheck: B7 is never written, so it is absent from the grid. eval_range (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:1841) materialises absent cells in a rectangle as Blank, NOT Number(0.0) — its own comment calls the zero-injection 'THE REAL DEFECT' — and collect_numbers_recursive (evaluator.rs:4132) has the arm `EvalResult::Blank => {}` at line 4140, so the blank is dropped rather than collected. The numeric population of B2:B8 is therefore 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 71 — six values, already ascending. fn_median (evaluator.rs:8777) sorts, sees len % 2 == 0, and returns (numbers[len/2 - 1] + numbers[len/2]) / 2 = (numbers[2] + numbers[3]) / 2 = (4 + 6) / 2 = 5.0, an exact integer in binary floating point.

tasks.intent: In E2, find the variable cost per unit: the slope of the least-squares straight line that predicts Cost (column C) from Units (column B) across the six production batches in rows 2 to 7. The Total row in row 8 is not a batch and must be left out.

distractor.why: SLOPE takes known_y first and known_x second (SLOPE(known_y, known_x)); writing the x range first regresses Units on Cost and returns 150000/3752750 = 0.03997068816, not 25. Two further traps the fixture now catches: the two-point shortcut =(C7-C2)/(B7-B2) reads 2240/90 = 24.888..., and =SLOPE(C2:C8,B2:B8) pulls in the Total row pair (300 units, 9390 cost) and returns 30.6654676.

tasks.handCheck: fn_slope (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:12623) pairs the two ranges, then returns sum((x-mean_x)*(y-mean_y)) / sum((x-mean_x)^2). x = 10,20,40,50,80,100, sum 300, mean_x = 50 exactly. y = 600,800,1300,1550,2300,2840, sum 9390, mean_y = 1565 exactly. dx = -40,-30,-10,0,30,50. dy = -965,-765,-265,-15,735,1275. (The line is Cost = 25*Units + 315, and only four of the six batches sit on it: B-01 is 285 above it and B-06 is 25 below it, so no pair of endpoints reproduces the fit.)

tasks.intent: In D2, calculate the fixed monthly payment on the loan described in B1:B4: the loan amount is in B1, the annual interest rate in B2, the term in years in B3 and the number of payments per year in B4. Use the monthly rate (annual rate divided by payments per year) and the total number of payments (years times payments per year). Payments are made at the END of each month, and nothing is left owing at the end of the term. The arrangement fee in B5 is paid up front in cash and is not financed, so it is not part of the loan amount. Keep PMT's own sign — the answer is a negative number — and round it to 2 decimals.
tasks.intentSv: Beräkna i D2 den fasta månadsbetalningen på lånet som beskrivs i B1:B4: lånebeloppet står i B1, årsräntan i B2, löptiden i år i B3 och antalet betalningar per år i B4. Använd månadsräntan (årsräntan delad med antalet betalningar per år) och det totala antalet betalningar (antal år gånger betalningar per år). Betalningarna sker i slutet av varje månad och lånet är helt återbetalt när löptiden är slut. Uppläggningsavgiften i B5 betalas kontant och ingår inte i lånebeloppet. Behåll PMT:s eget tecken — svaret ska vara negativt — och avrunda till 2 decimaler.

distractor.why: It feeds the ANNUAL rate 0.06 into a formula that still counts 60 monthly periods, so it charges 6% per month. PMT(0.06,60,240000) = -14850.17, more than three times the true payment of -4639.87. Two further traps the fixture catches: folding the 2500 arrangement fee into the principal as B1+B5 finances money that is actually paid in cash and gives -4688.20; and paying at the start of each month, =ROUND(PMT(B2/B4,B3*B4,B1,0,1),2), gives -4616.79.

tasks.handCheck: rate = 0.06/12 = 0.005 exactly; nper = 5*12 = 60; pv = 240000; fv = 0 (omitted); type = 0 (omitted, i.e. end of period). fn_pmt (core/engine/src/evaluator.rs:8945) takes the args in the order rate, nper, pv, [fv], [type], computes pvif = (1+rate)^nper = 1.005^60 = 1.3488501525493075, then pmt = rate*(pv*pvif + fv)/(pvif - 1) = 0.005*240000*1.3488501525493075/0.3488501525493075 = 1618.6201830591690/0.3488501525493075 = 4639.872367062785, and returns -pmt because type != 1. So PMT = -4639.872367062785 (recomputed independently in IEEE-754 double arithmetic, not taken from the author). fn_round (evaluator.rs:4899) computes (num * 10^digits).round() / 10^digits = (-463987.2367062785).round()/100 = -463987/100 = -4639.87. Not a halfway case, so the round-half-away-from-zero convention does not bite.

tasks.intent: In D2, calculate the net present value of the project in A1:B7 using a discount rate of 10% per year, rounded to 2 decimals. The Year 0 outlay in B2 happens today, so it is already at present value and must NOT be discounted; only the Year 1 to Year 5 cash flows in B3:B7 get discounted, the first of them by one year.

distractor.why: NPV discounts its FIRST value by one full period, so putting the Year 0 outlay inside the range treats -50000 as if it were spent at the end of Year 1 and pushes all five later flows one year further out as well. It returns 12863.63 instead of 14149.99 — an error of 1286.36 that still looks like a plausible NPV, which is why this mistake survives review. A second trap: subtracting the outlay, =ROUND(NPV(0.1,B3:B7)-B2,2), double-counts its sign and returns 64149.99.
